newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-Nazi Priebke faces Italy justice for second time.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi Priebke faces Italy justice for second time.

text.p: Former Nazi German SS captain Erich Priebke, accused of complicity in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, faced Italian justice for the second time in a year on Monday.

The proceedings in a heavily fortified courtroom in a prison outside Rome began by discussing the legal position of Karl Hass, a former SS major accused in the same 1944 massacre of 335 men and boys in 1944 in Rome's Ardeatine Caves.
Hass and Priebke are accused of complicity but while Priebke is facing a re-trial, Hass is facing his first trial.
Both men admit to having taken part in the massacre, but say they were following orders and would have been executed if they had refused to act.

Priebke was found guilty last August of involvement in the massacre in caves south of Rome but was ordered to be released under a statute of limitation. The verdict, which sparked a storm of protest, was quashed on appeal and a retrial ordered.
The military court began the proceedings by hearing military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano's request that Hass be tried together with Priebke.
The court retired to decide whether one or two trials should be held. "There is a procedural complication," Intelisano told reporters during the break.
"The complication is connected to the rank of the military judge because under (Italian) legislation the rank of the military judge is connected to the rank of the man on trial," the prosecutor said.
"Hass is a major while Priebke is captain. Now the court has to decide about the putting the two together," Intelisano said.
Court sources said they expected that if the military panel decided to join the two cases, the court would then immediately begin procedures involving Priebke.
Hass originally returned to Italy as a witness at Priebke's first trial and is currently under house arrest after fracturing his pelvis trying to flee over a hotel balcony and avoid testifying.
Hass was not present in the courtroom when the proceedings began.
But lawyers said Priebke had travelled to the court in Rebibbia prison in the capital's eastern outskirts and would probably enter the courtroom later.
Priebke, who was extradited from Argentina in November 1995, and admits he shot two victims in the massacre.
The shootings came as a reprisal for a partisan bomb attack in which 33 troops loyal to the Nazis died.
Priebke has been living in a monastery south of Rome since he was released from prison to house arrest earlier this year.

"For me it was an action of war, I had to obey the order like all the others," Priebke told Il Giornale newspaper on Sunday, adding that he had not thought any more about the killings once the war ended.
Priebke fled to Argentina in 1948 after escaping from a British prisoner of war camp in Italy.

When the first verdict freeing Priebke was handed down last August, protesters besieged the courtroom and stopped Priebke from leaving until Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick ordered his re-arrest based on an extradition request by Germany.
The extradition request was turned down in February but in the meantime the original verdict had been thrown out on appeal.
